title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
abstract: Discrete time crystals are non-equilibrium phases of matter with spatiotemporal order and a response that breaks the time-translation symmetry of a periodic external drive. Interactions, spatial disorder and correlated random driving can in theory stabilize this order. In experiments, however, coupling to the environment limits the time crystal lifetime. Here we use stochastic local bit-flip error correction to prolong the time-crystalline response of a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting quantum processor, using a repetition code with distances three and five on a honeycomb lattice with up to 68 physical qubits. Even though ancilla qubits, midcircuit syndrome measurements and decoding increase the required quantum and classical resources, the stochastic drive increases the memory decay time by a factor of up to two. At late times we observe that recovery stabilizes spatial order across the lattice. The spin-configuration distributions explain this separation, as recovery suppresses disagreeing bonds while broadening occupies completely reversed states. Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction. Our results show that local bit-flip error correction can preserve time-crystalline memory over more drive cycles than the bare dynamics.
summary: This research demonstrates that applying local bit-flip error correction protocols can significantly extend the memory lifetime of time-crystalline order in a noisy quantum simulation. By implementing these error correction circuits on a superconducting processor, the authors show that the system's ability to maintain spatiotemporal order is robustly protected, confirming the utility of QEC for stabilizing exotic quantum phases.
main_problem: The primary goal is to extend the operational lifetime of time-crystalline memory in a noisy quantum processor by implementing local error correction protocols.
main_result: Local bit-flip error correction significantly prolongs the memory decay time of the time-crystalline response, increasing it by a factor of up to two compared to bare dynamics.
method: The study uses superconducting quantum processors to simulate a driven Ising model, applying stochastic local bit-flip error correction (repetition codes of distances three and five) to mitigate environmental decoherence.
model_or_system: The system is a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model simulated on a superconducting quantum processor using a honeycomb lattice. The dynamics are governed by a Floquet drive, and the error correction involves ancilla qubits and syndrome measurements.
key_observables: Temporal memory decay ($	au$), spatial alignment ($A_Z$), connected correlations ($G_c(d)$), domain-wall fraction ($D$), and quantum negativity ($\mathcal{N}$).
important_parameters: The error correction distances (3-site and 5-site), the probability ($p$) of activating the stochastic drive/correction, and the lattice size (up to 68 physical qubits).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the effectiveness of local bit-flip error correction and assumes that the measured physical time is an accurate conversion from the cycle-domain decay scale.
figures_summary: Figures compare connected correlations and domain-wall fractions for bare vs. recovered dynamics, showing recovery maintains order; Figure 2 shows temporal memory loss curves; Figure 3 compares error distributions ($W$ and $K$); Figure 5 compares entanglement (Negativity) across protocols.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the time-crystal model and the challenge of decoherence. It then introduces the error correction methodology, comparing the decay of temporal and spatial order under bare dynamics versus various local recovery protocols. Finally, it quantifies the improvement in memory lifetime and spatial stabilization achieved by the conditional correction.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges the physics of non-equilibrium quantum matter (time crystals) with the practical challenges of quantum computation, demonstrating how QEC techniques can stabilize exotic quantum phases against noise.
